text: Some men came down from Judea and began teaching the brothers, "Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved."

This brought Paul and Barnabas into sharp dissension and debate with them, so the brothers appointed Paul and Barnabas, along with some of the others, to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and elders about this question.

versions.text: This brought Paul and Barnabas into sharp dissension and debate with them, so the church appointed Paul and Barnabas, along with some of the others, to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and elders about this question.
versions.explanation: The Greek has only an unnamed plural subject (ἔταξαν). Rendering it "the church" anticipates and duplicates verse 3 ("Sent on their way by the church"); "the brothers" keeps the reference natural and consistent with verse 1 without adding a term the Greek does not use here.

text: Sent on their way by the church, they traveled through Phoenicia and Samaria, telling in detail how the Gentiles had turned to God, and they brought great joy to all the brothers.
When they arrived in Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church, the apostles, and the elders, and they reported everything God had done through them.
But some believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees stood up and said, "They must be circumcised and required to keep the law of Moses."
So the apostles and the elders met together to consider this matter.

After a long debate, Peter stood up and said to them: "Brothers, you know that in the early days God chose me from among you, so that the Gentiles might hear the word of the gospel from my lips and believe.
And God, who knows the heart, testified in their favor by giving them the Holy Spirit, just as he did to us.
He made no distinction between us and them, for he cleansed their hearts by faith.
So then, why are you putting God to the test by laying on the necks of the disciples a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?
No, we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, in the very same way they are."
The whole assembly fell silent as they listened to Barnabas and Paul recount all the signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them.
When they had finished, James spoke up: "Brothers, listen to me.
Simeon has described how God first showed his concern by taking from the Gentiles a people for his name.

versions.text: Simeon has described how God first visited the Gentiles to take from them a people for his name.
versions.explanation: In the Greek, ἐπεσκέψατο has no stated object; the point is that God acted graciously in order to take a people from among the Gentiles. "Visited the Gentiles... from them" both supplies an object not in the text and creates a slightly redundant double reference.

text: And this agrees with the words of the prophets, as it is written:
"'After this I will return and rebuild the fallen tent of David; I will rebuild its ruins and set it up again,
so that the rest of humanity may seek the Lord, even all the Gentiles who bear my name, says the Lord, who does these things,

versions.text: so that the rest of humanity may seek the Lord—all the Gentiles who are called by my name, says the Lord, who does these things,
versions.explanation: "All the Gentiles" is a second subject of the verb "may seek" (joined by καί), not an appositional restatement. The dash makes it sound like a mere explanation of "the rest of humanity"; "even all the Gentiles" preserves the joined subject and reads smoothly aloud.

text: known from of old.'
Therefore my judgment is that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who are turning to God,
but should write to them to abstain from what has been polluted by idols, from sexual immorality, from the meat of strangled animals, and from blood.
For from ancient generations Moses has had those who proclaim him in every city, since he is read aloud in the synagogues every Sabbath."

Then the apostles and the elders, with the whole church, decided to choose men from among themselves and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas: Judas called Barsabbas and Silas, leading men among the brothers.
They sent this letter with them: "The apostles and the elders, your brothers, to the brothers among the Gentiles in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia: Greetings.
We have heard that some men went out from us, without any authorization from us, and unsettled you with their words, troubling your minds.
So we came to a unanimous decision to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,
men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Therefore we are sending Judas and Silas, who will tell you the same things by word of mouth.
For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us not to lay on you any burden beyond these necessary things:
that you abstain from food sacrificed to idols, from blood, from the meat of strangled animals, and from sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell."
So they were sent off and went down to Antioch, where they gathered the congregation together and delivered the letter.
When it was read, the people rejoiced at its encouragement.
Judas and Silas, who were themselves prophets, said much to encourage and strengthen the brothers.
After spending some time there, they were sent off in peace by the brothers to those who had sent them.
But Silas decided to remain there.
Paul and Barnabas stayed on in Antioch, where they and many others taught and proclaimed the word of the Lord.
Some days later Paul said to Barnabas, "Let us go back and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, and see how they are doing."
Barnabas wanted to take John, also called Mark, along with them,
but Paul insisted that they should not take along someone who had deserted them in Pamphylia and had not gone on with them to the work.
The disagreement was so sharp that they parted company. Barnabas took Mark and sailed for Cyprus,
while Paul chose Silas and set out, commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord.
He traveled through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.
